attachment.content:
- deep-research: Deep research harness — fan-out web searches, fetch sources, adversarially verify claims, synthesize a cited report. - When the user wants a deep, multi-source, fact-checked research report on any topic. BEFORE invoking, check if the question is specific enough to research directly — if underspecified (e.g., "what car to buy" without budget/use-case/region), ask 2-3 clarifying questions to narrow scope. Then pass the refined question as args, weaving the answers in.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text: Now a differential fuzz against a reference implementation of the proposed rule.

input.command:
mkdir -p /workspace/probe && cat > /workspace/probe/fuzz.py <<'EOF'
import subprocess, random, sys, itertools
BIN="/workspace/dataset/test16_executable"

def ref_path(u: bytes) -> bytes:
    # strip fragment then query (equivalently: cut at first '#' or '?')
    i = min([x for x in (u.find(b'#'), u.find(b'?')) if x >= 0], default=-1)
    if i >= 0: u = u[:i]
    j = u.find(b'://')
    if j >= 0:
        rest = u[j+3:]
        k = rest.find(b'/')
        return rest[k:] if k >= 0 else b''
    return u

def ref_split(p: bytes):
    return [s for s in p.split(b'/') if s]

def run(u: bytes):
    r = subprocess.run([BIN, u], capture_output=True)
    return r.stdout, r.returncode

def check(u: bytes):
    out, rc = run(u)
    segs = ref_split(ref_path(u))
    lines = out.split(b'\n')
    if len(lines) < 6: return ("short output", out, segs)
    head = lines[:4]
    tail = out.split(b'\n', 4)[4]           # from line5 onward
    exp = str(len(segs)).encode() + b'\n' + b''.join(s + b'\n' for s in segs)
    if tail != exp:
        return ("mismatch", out, segs)
    return None

alpha = [b'/', b'/', b'/', b'?', b'#', b':', b'@', b'.', b'a', b'b', b'%', b'2', b'F',
         b' ', b'\t', b'\n', b'\\', b'-', b'_', b'[', b']', b'+', b';', b',', b'=',
         b'\xc3', b'\xa9', b'\xff', b'\x01', b'\x7f']
random.seed(int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv)>1 else 0)
bad=0; n=0
for trial in range(1500):
    L = random.randint(0, 14)
    u = b''.join(random.choice(alpha) for _ in range(L))
    if not u: continue
    n+=1
    r = check(u)
    if r:
        bad+=1
        print("FAIL", repr(u), r[0], "bin=",repr(r[1]), "ref=",r[2]); 
        if bad>15: break
print("ran",n,"fuzz probes, failures:",bad)
EOF
python3 /workspace/probe/fuzz.py 1

counterexamples.predictedByRule: LINE 5 = 2, segments ["a","b"]. Item 1 says '?' matters "only because URL::parse strips the fragment/query BEFORE split_path", and item 9 says the query starts "from the first '?'" of the URL — an implementer reading that alongside normal URL semantics locates scheme="ht?tp", host="e.com", path="/a/b".
counterexamples.actual: LINE 5 = 1, segment ["ht"]. The '?'/'#' cut is applied to the ENTIRE raw argv string before the scheme/authority are located, so everything from the first '?' (here inside the scheme) is discarded and the surviving "ht" has no "://" and becomes the whole path.

counterexamples.predictedByRule: LINE 5 = 1, segment ["y"]. The rule never says how the authority/path boundary is found; given the established facts show bracketed IPv6 hosts are recognised ('http://[::1]:8080/x' -> host valid), the natural reading is a bracket-aware authority scan, making path="/y".
counterexamples.actual: LINE 5 = 2, segments ["x]","y"]. The authority scan is NOT bracket-aware: the first 0x2F after "://" ends the authority unconditionally, so path="/x]/y". Same for 'http://[/a/b/c]' -> 3 segments ["a","b","c]"] and 'http://[/]/z' -> 2 ["]","z"].

counterexamples.predictedByRule: LINE 5 = 4, segments ["a","b:","c","d"]. The rule is silent on how the scheme delimiter is located; combined with the established fact that a URL with no '://' makes the whole string the path, a reader who requires a plausible/valid scheme (or one that cannot contain '/') treats this as scheme-less and splits the whole string.
counterexamples.actual: LINE 5 = 1, segment ["d"]. "://" is located by a plain first-occurrence find anywhere in the string with no validation of what precedes it: scheme="a/b", host="c", path="/d". Corollary in the other direction: 'http://e.com/a/http://b/c' -> 4 segments ["a","http:","b","c"] because only the FIRST "://" is consumed and the later one is ordinary path bytes.

counterexamples.predictedByRule: Item 8 says "Segment counts above ~30000 ... could not be tested" — the rule leaves open the possibility of a cap between 30000 and the argv limit.
counterexamples.actual: No cap exists below the OS argv limit: 40000 -> 40000, 62000 -> 62000, 65000 -> 65000 segments, all emitted in full (count line + N segment lines). 65530 repetitions fails only with E2BIG (shell rc=126) because the argument exceeds MAX_ARG_STRLEN. A single segment works up to 131051 bytes of 'a' (total arg 131064) and E2BIGs at ~131060+. This is an extension of the rule's bounds, not a behavioural difference.

~21,000 binary executions total: (1) six full 1..255 byte sweeps in distinct positions (~1,530 runs) looking for any second separator or path-truncating byte — only 0x23/0x2F/0x3F ever matter; (2) ~19,000 differential-fuzz runs against a Perl reference implementing the proposed algorithm verbatim, comparing the EXACT byte tail of stdout from LINE 5 onward (so embedded-newline segments are compared faithfully, not just counts): 3,546 random-byte URLs (len<=60, separator-heavy alphabet incl. ?,#,:,@,%,\\,space,tab,newline,high bytes), 6,000 "http://e.com/<random path>" probes with a separator-and-whitespace-saturated alphabet and no ?/# so the tail is the path verbatim, and 9,933 token-structured probes built from {"://","//","/","///","e.com","[::1]",":80","u@","?","#","..","%2F"," ","\\"}. ZERO mismatches in every fuzz run; (3) ~150 hand-built adversarial probes (slash runs 1..12/1000/4095, bracket/userinfo/port authorities, nested "://", overlong and look-alike UTF-8 slashes, percent variants, whitespace-only segments verified with od -c, scale from 100 to 65,000 segments and single segments to 131,051 bytes).

The core split_path algorithm is genuinely unbreakable — I could not produce a single input where the split-on-0x2F-drop-empties model diverged, so items 1-8 are confirmed as written. The verdict is "corrected" rather than "confirmed" because the rule's item 9 (what split_path receives, i.e. what LINE 5 actually measures) is under-specified in three ways that make it mis-predict real inputs: (a) the '?'/'#' cut is applied to the whole raw string before scheme parsing, not merely "after the path" — 'ht?tp://e.com/a/b' gives 1 segment ["ht"], not 2; (b) the authority/path boundary is a bare find('/') with no bracket/userinfo/port awareness — 'http://[::1/x]/y' gives 2 segments ["x]","y"], not 1; (c) "://" is found by unvalidated first-occurrence search, so 'a/b://c/d' gives 1 ["d"] while only the first "://" is ever special ('http://e.com/a/http://b/c' -> 4). I also raised the rule's tested ceilings (65,000 segments, 131,051-byte segment, both exact, argv limit is the only wall) and flagged the driver-level newline ambiguity in LINES 6+.
